Importune
im-por-TUNE
verb
From the Latin importunus, “troublesome, unfit, out of season” (in-, “not,” + portus, “a harbour” — that which affords no landing-place); hence to press a request without ceasing, to urge and urge again until the thing is granted.

Biblical Definition

To importune is to press a petition without leaving off — to ask, and ask again, and refuse to be dismissed. The Authorized Version carries the noun in the Lord’s own parable of the friend at midnight: “yet because of his importunity he will rise and give him as many as he needeth” (Luk 11:8). The neighbour will not stir for friendship’s sake; he will stir because the knocking will not stop. So also the widow of Luk 18, who wearied an unjust judge by “her continual coming” (Luk 18:5) until he avenged her. Both parables are arguments from the lesser to the greater, and both are given for the same declared end: “that men ought always to pray, and not to faint” (Luk 18:1). The point is emphatically not that God is a grudging neighbour or an unjust judge who must be worn down. It is the opposite: if reluctance yields to persistence, how much more shall the Father who delights to give? “And shall not God avenge his own elect, which cry day and night unto him?” (Luk 18:7). Importunity is therefore not a lever upon God but a mark upon His elect — they are the ones who cry day and night. It is Jacob at Peniel refusing to loose his hold, and the Syrophenician woman answering the Lord’s own hard word with faith. The persevering asker is not manufacturing the answer; he is being conformed to a Giver who has already resolved to give.

Webster 1828 Definition

To press or urge a request with troublesome frequency; to solicit without ceasing until the thing is obtained.

expand to see more

IMPORTUNE, to request with urgency; to press with solicitation; to urge with frequent application.

IMPORTUNITY, pressing solicitation; urgent request; incessant or frequent application.

From Latin importunus, “troublesome, affording no harbour” — a suit that will not be put off.

The friend at midnight receives because of his importunity (Luk 11:8).

The widow’s continual coming wearied the unjust judge (Luk 18:5).

Key Scripture

Luk 11:8 — "I say unto you, Though he will not rise and give him, because he is his friend, yet because of his importunity he will rise and give him as many as he needeth."

Luk 18:1 — "And he spake a parable unto them to this end, that men ought always to pray, and not to faint;"

Luk 18:5 — "Yet because this widow troubleth me, I will avenge her, lest by her continual coming she weary me."

Luk 18:7 — "And shall not God avenge his own elect, which cry day and night unto him, though he bear long with them?"

Modern Corruption

Importunity is bent into a technique — the name-it-and-claim-it doctrine that treats persistence as leverage over a reluctant God.

expand to see more

The chief corruption is the prosperity teacher’s reading, in which importunity becomes a spiritual mechanism. Ask with sufficient force, decree with sufficient confidence, refuse to accept the word no, and heaven must yield — as though the Father were the unjust judge of the parable rather than its foil. This inverts the Lord’s argument exactly. He does not say God is like the surly neighbour; He says that if even a surly neighbour yields to knocking, the Father who already knows what you need will not be found less generous. The name-it-and-claim-it scheme also quietly relocates the object of prayer: the friend at midnight asked bread for a traveller, and the widow asked justice, while the modern petitioner is taught to importune for houses, cars, and healings on demand. When the goods do not arrive, the blame falls on the asker’s faith, and a doctrine meant to comfort the persevering saint becomes a whip for the grieving one.

There is a quieter corruption on the other side: the professing believer who does not importune at all, having concluded that since God has decreed the end there is no use in asking. But the same God who ordains the end ordains the crying of His elect day and night as the appointed means of it. Prayer does not change God’s mind; it is the instrument by which He accomplishes what He purposed, and by which He makes His children like Himself in the asking. Hence the parable’s stated aim — that men ought always to pray, and not to faint. Importunity is the posture of Jacob, who would not let go, and of the widow, who would not go away; and the Father who delights to give His Spirit to them that ask has already bound Himself to answer, in His own time and in His own better way, every petition that faith presses at His door.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The word means to press a request without ceasing until it is granted.

expand to see more

Importune — Latin importunus, “troublesome, affording no harbour.”

It names the suit that gives no landing-place, no room to put the asker off.

The friend at midnight receives for his importunity, not his friendship (Luk 11:8).

The widow’s continual coming wore out an unjust judge (Luk 18:5).

Both parables argue upward: how much more the Father of the elect (Luk 18:7).

Usage

"Importunity is not leverage upon God but the mark of the elect who cry day and night."

"Christ gave the parable that men ought always to pray, and not to faint."

"The unjust judge is the parable’s foil, never its picture of the Father."
